chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 421 to 430, Peyanar's mixed mullai decade (முல்லை விரவுப் பத்து): the man held from going by her shoulders and her tears, the friend dissuading him with the rains and the crying son, the hurried drive home past doves and mullai, and the choice between the king's war and the wife, renounced in one poem, made conditional in another, and ended by the rains in a third.

421.reading: The man says that the going he had planned was stopped by the full, bamboo-smooth shoulders of the young daughter of the chief of the poor scrubland, where at evening the watchmen throw their white missiles and the hare hiding in the fragrant flowered woodland bolts.
421.nuance: The journey is not refused by argument: her shoulders 'block' it (விலங்கின), as if they stood across the road. The hare driven from its cover by the watchmen is the one creature in the poem that does leave; the man, by contrast, stays. What the watchmen throw (வெண்காழ், a white hard thing, perhaps sling-stones or pointed sticks) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a planned departure is given up

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man speaks of the girl in the third person, to no one named, perhaps to his own heart

422.reading: The man says that if they drive the tall chariot fast, its strong-legged horses scattering the flowers of the long-stemmed mullai and the thalavam, she with rows of bangles on her forearm will not suffer.
422.nuance: Her suffering is measured by his speed: the conditional (செல்லின்) makes the charioteer's haste the remedy for her pain, and the scattered mullai and thalavam, the flowers of the waiting land, are crushed by the very return they wait for.

thinai_evidence.note: the man hurries home to the waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man urges his charioteer (pira) on the way home

423.reading: The friend tells the man that the great clouds have thundered and let fall their drops, yet he is set on going while her bright brow turns pale; they cannot bear to be left by him, and her kohl-dark eyes, fine as chosen flowers, are already full of tears.
423.nuance: The friend's argument is the season itself: a man who leaves when the rain has already come breaks the order by which men return in the rains. The rain is mullai's time set inside a scene of departure; the mixing is of time, not of native things.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is preparing to leave

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the friend speaks for the woman (யாமே) to the man about to leave

424.reading: The friend warns the man that if he goes, making pale the bright brow of the beloved young daughter of the chief of the woodland, his dear son, like a lotus opening its bud in clear water, will now cry for the breast.
424.nuance: The friend names the wife as her father's daughter, as if reminding the husband from whose house he took her, and then names the son as his (நின் புதல்வன்): the cost of going falls first on the child, whose mother's grief will fail him at the breast.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend dissuades the man from leaving

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the friend speaks to the man who means to leave; the son shows the stage is karpu

iraicchi.act: the hen dove croons to give her mate pleasure
iraicchi.sense: the man, hearing a mate call to her partner, knows his wife waits calling for him, and so hurries home

425.reading: The man tells his charioteer that if he drives the tall chariot fast through the woodland, where the dun-backed hen dove croons like the drummers of kings to please her mate, it will be easy to end their sore pain.
425.nuance: The 'our' pain (எமக்கு) is shared: his road-weariness and her waiting are ended by one act, the fast drive.

thinai_evidence.note: the man hurries home to end the waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man urges his charioteer (pira) on the return

426.reading: The man tells his fair-browed wife that, giving up the hard task of the king of the conquering spear, he has now stopped going to the hard battle where that king sets the drums thundering and overcomes kings.
426.nuance: The war he renounces is painted at its height, drums and conquered kings, in the same breath as the refusal, so the giving up is shown as a real cost and not an easy choice.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gives up a departure for the king's war

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man speaks to his wife (நன்னுதல்)

427.reading: The friend tells the wide-eyed girl that because she would not let him go, saying this is the season that meets the rains, he gave up the going, sending word that he would not come to the war camp of the fighting king.
427.nuance: The girl's argument was the season (காரெதிர் பொழுது), the same argument the friend uses in 423; here it has worked. Whose 'not coming' வாரான் அவன் reports is open: most simply, the man's refusal of the king's summons.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gives up a departure

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the friend tells the woman (மடந்தை) that her plea has kept the man home

428.reading: The man tells his wife that the roaring cloud, bending its fine bow across the sky, has begun to pour so that chariots cannot move; the great task the king sent him on is over, and he has begun to stay and care for her.
428.nuance: The rain does the work of the return: it halts the chariots of war, so the king's task ends because the season forbids it, and the same rain that would have tormented a waiting wife now marks the start of his staying (புறந்தர).

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come and the man is home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man, back from the king's work, speaks to his wife

429.reading: The man tells the woman of thick dark hair that if she puts away her pallor he would go to win the king's war, the king whose untrained elephant shattered the fortress of his foes with its conquering flags.
429.nuance: The condition is one she cannot meet: her pallor comes from his going, so 'if you give up your pallor' (பசப்பு நீ விடின்) makes the journey wait on a cure that only his staying brings. The wish particle தில் keeps the going a wish, not a plan.

thinai_evidence.note: the man seeks leave to depart

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man speaks to the woman (பல்லிருங் கூந்தல்) asking leave

430.reading: The man says that the daughter of the chief of the wooded land, where on the high rock the short-stemmed konrai spreads bright petals like beaten gold, has wept her fill, and so he gives up the going.
430.nuance: The konrai in bloom is the flower of the rains, the season of return; he gives up going in the very season when a man should come home. ஆன்றிசின் may mean she has wept abundantly or be a plea that she stop weeping; either way her tears decide.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gives up a departure because she weeps

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man speaks of the woman in the third person, to no one named

links.note: In 424 the friend warns the man that his son will cry for the breast if he goes; in Akananuru 66 the crying son actually stops the man's chariot on the way to another wedding.
links.teaches: The friend's threat in Ainkurunuru 424 is the plan of which Akananuru 66 shows the working: the son as the one claim a departing husband cannot argue with was a recognised move, used against a journey for the king's work and against a journey to another woman alike.

links.note: In Natrinai 166 the husband himself tells his wife that their son has learnt to play and asks why he should part from her.
links.teaches: Natrinai gives the husband's own voice answering the friend's argument of Ainkurunuru 424, so the son as a reason to stay worked from both sides of the speech situation: urged on the man by the friend, and taken up by him unprompted.

links.note: In 426 the man has given up the king's hard task to stay with his wife; in Akananuru 214 the man in the camp says the war is their own duty (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) while imagining her lonely rainy evening.
links.teaches: Held together, the poems show that the mullai husband's bond to the king's war was not fixed: one binds himself to it despite her loneliness, the other renounces it for her brow, so akam staged a real choice between royal service and the wife.

links.note: In 428 the rains, with the rainbow, halt the chariots and end the king's task; in Akananuru 84 the rains and the rainbow come but the angry king refuses tribute and moves his army on.
links.teaches: The convention that the rains end a campaign, which 428 takes for granted, is broken in Akananuru 84 by one king's anger, so the rainbow is a promise of return that only the king can keep or cancel.

links.note: In 426 the man has given up the king's war; in 429 he says he would go to it if the woman puts away her pallor.
links.teaches: Within one decade the poet sets a flat refusal of royal service beside a conditional consent to it whose condition, her pallor gone, is undone by the going itself, so 429 reads as a refusal phrased as a promise.

links.note: Both men give up a planned journey because of the woman; in 421 her shoulders 'block' the going, in Akananuru 5 her silent grieving and the son at her breast.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru keeps only the outcome and one bodily sign of what Akananuru 5 unfolds as a scene of silent pleading, so the short form shows that the persuasion could be left wholly implied once the convention of the abandoned journey was known.

links.note: In Akananuru 254 the waiting wife watches the house dove fly with its mate while the man drives home; in 425 the man on the road hears the forest dove croon for its mate.
links.teaches: Together the poems place the paired dove at both ends of the return journey, in the wife's courtyard and on the husband's road, so the same creature serves as the sign by which each partner reads the other's longing.

links.note: Both dissuade the man from leaving, in the friend's voice on Parimelazhagar's reading of the couplet: the Kural argues from her survival, 423 from the rain already falling and her filled eyes.
links.teaches: The two show that the dissuasion of a departure had two set arguments, the season and her life, and the Kural keeps only the harsher second, while the Ainkurunuru friend leans on the order of the seasons that a man who leaves in the rains breaks.

source_issues: The colophon gives முல்லை for the whole decade with no thurai; seven poems (421, 423, 424, 426, 427, 429, 430) turn on a departure planned, dissuaded or given up, which by uri is paalai, and are marked so in thinai.
421: what the watchmen throw (வெண்காழ்) is not certain.
430: ஆன்றிசின் can be read as 'has wept her fill' or as a plea to stop weeping.
